extracted.intended_audience: users of the Metamath program and mathematicians learning formal formal-proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for encoding axiomatic theories and constructing/verifying formal proofs in the Metamath language and Proof Assistant; includes CLI commands, proof-display options, and unification/assignment workflow for building proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom schemes (A1, A2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A1 and A2 are properly called “axiom schemes,” but we will refer to them as “axioms” for brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms can represent infinitely many instances via schemes; treat axiom schemes as the source truths from which theorems are derived. When encoding an axiom scheme in Metamath, express it as an $a (axiomatic assertion) statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus Ponens (MP) inference rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and (P -> Q) are theorems (where P and Q are wff s), then Q is also a theorem. The second part of this definition is called the modus ponens (MP) rule of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MP is the fundamental rule to obtain new theorems from old ones; in Metamath it is encoded as an assertion (e.g., mp) whose mandatory hypotheses must be satisfied and which is used as a proof step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is a sequence of one or more theorems, each of which is either an axiom or the result of modus ponens applied to two previous theorems in the sequence, and the last of which is the theorem being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing proofs in Metamath, ensure each proof step corresponds to either an axiom or an application of a referenced assertion whose mandatory hypotheses are provided earlier in the sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove theorem schemes rather than single instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Our theorem is more properly called a 'theorem scheme,' for it represents an infinite number of theorems, one for each possible term t. Rarely do we prove actual theorems, since by proving schemes we can prove an infinite number of theorems in one fell swoop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure assertions and proofs to be schematic (use metavariables) so single proofs cover infinitely many concrete instances; to obtain an actual proof, substitute a concrete term for metavariables throughout the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose axioms that are trivial and obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Stating the trivial and obvious is a goal to strive for in any axiomatic system. From trivial and obvious truths that everyone agrees upon, we can prove results that are not so obvious yet have absolute faith in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer minimal, simple, and evidently acceptable axioms; eliminate redundant axioms when they can be derived as theorems to simplify the axiom set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly specify syntactic categories (term, wff)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath does not know what a 'term' or a 'wff' is. In Metamath, the specification of the ways in which we can combine symbols to obtain terms and wff s are like little axioms in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define formation rules as $a assertions (e.g., tze, tpl, weq, wim) so that Metamath can verify constructions; these auxiliary axioms use the same notation as 'real' axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: $c and $v declarations (constants and variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath tokens $c and $v each declare a list of user-defined tokens, called 'math symbols,' that the database will reference later on. The $c statement declares 'constants' and the $v statement declares 'variables' (metavariables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use $c for tokens that must match themselves and cannot be substituted; use $v for metavariables that may be substituted. Declaring both improves error checking and allows redeclaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: $f, $e, $a, $p statement roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The token $f specifies a 'variable-type hypothesis' (floating hypothesis), $e specifies a 'logical hypothesis' (essential hypothesis), $a specifies an 'axiomatic assertion,' and $p specifies a 'provable assertion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use $f to declare variable type constraints (exactly two math symbols: a constant then a variable), $e for needed hypotheses, $a for axioms, and $p for theorems with an associated proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory hypotheses and how they are determined
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated with each assertion is a set of hypotheses that must be satisfied in order for the assertion to be used in a proof. Among those hypotheses whose scope includes the assertion, $e hypotheses are always mandatory and $f hypotheses are mandatory when they share their variable with the assertion or its $e hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand mandatory hypotheses' determination rules (detailed in referenced sections); use show statement or show proof to inspect a statement's mandatory hypotheses and their RPN order when debugging proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ${ and $} to delimit hypothesis scope (blocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath brackets, ${ and $}, define a 'block' that delimits the scope of any hypothesis contained between them. Sometimes we need to make a hypothesis relevant to only certain assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encapsulate local hypotheses inside blocks so they are only mandatory for statements within the block; assertions ($a and $p) are not affected by ${ $} scope and are globally referenceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are RPN sequences operating on a stack
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are familiar with reverse Polish notation (RPN)... Each hypothesis label in the proof is pushed onto the RPN stack as it is encountered. Each assertion label pops off the stack as many entries as the referenced assertion has mandatory hypotheses. Variable substitutions are computed ... and the referenced assertion itself is pushed onto the stack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or verifying proofs, understand the stack-based construction: at the end there must be exactly one stack entry equal to the asserted formula. This explains the compact label-based proof representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath proof-display modes and qualifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath program will convert compact proof notation into readable forms using show proof. You can request different levels of detail: lemmon-style display (/lemmon), tree-style, /all to include $f hypotheses and explicit constructions, /renumber to renumber displayed steps, /detailed_step to inspect substitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use /lemmon for explicit step-by-step display, /renumber to show essential steps in human-friendly order, /all to see full construction including $f steps, and /detailed_step <n> to examine substitutions performed at a particular step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath reads syntax but does not verify proofs on read
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are any syntax errors in the database, Metamath will let you know when it reads in the file. The one thing that Metamath does not check when reading in a database is that all proofs are correct, because this would slow it down too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After editing, explicitly run 'verify proof *' (or targeted verify) to ensure all proofs are correct; rely on verify proof to detect incorrect proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logging to capture Metamath output
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often useful to save the information that the Metamath program displays on the screen. You can save everything that happens on the screen by opening a log file (open log <file>), and close it with close log.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open a log before reading databases or making changes so you can inspect errors and proof displays later; log files are ordinary ASCII and handy for copy/paste of proof output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof Assistant workflow: work backwards and assign steps
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof is developed with the Proof Assistant by working backwards, starting with the theorem to be proved, and assigning each unknown step with a theorem or hypothesis until no more unknown steps remain. The Proof Assistant will not let you make an assignment unless it can be 'unified' with the unknown step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interactively assign statements to unknowns, prefer assigning in reverse order (later unknowns first) to reduce renumbering churn, and use show new_proof to inspect the evolving proof. The Assistant enforces unifiability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification choices and temporary variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When assigning a statement, the Assistant may present multiple possible unifications (substitution choices). Temporary variables (e.g., $2, $6) stand for unknown symbol sequences until eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect proposed unifications carefully; reject incorrect ones (they often yield meaningless fragments). You may defer unification (quit) and unify later interactively. Aim to eliminate temporary variables in the essential part of the proof so the Assistant can auto-fill remaining details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty substitution option affects unification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Metamath language allows empty symbol sequences to be substituted for variables, but by default this feature is turned off in the Proof Assistant. set empty_substitution on/off toggles this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turning on empty_substitution increases ambiguous unifications (empty substitutions are another possibility); leave it off unless you need to allow empty sequences (rare). If on, be prepared to choose among more unification options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve command to auto-fill steps
rubrics_metrics.description: The improve command can fill in many missing steps automatically. It only tries statements that introduce no new variables in their hypotheses (limited applicability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After eliminating essential unknowns, run 'improve all' to let Metamath find short proofs for remaining steps; verify afterwards with 'verify proof' since improve doesn't detect certain violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save new_proof to persist the constructed proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proof Assistant's save new_proof command will save the proof in the database (source buffer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finishing a proof and using improve, use SAVE/ save new_proof to write the proof back into the source file (or manually insert the displayed proof). Unsaved changes will trigger a warning on exit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof construction rules are purely symbol-matching
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules used in verifying a proof are not based on any built-in syntax of the symbol sequence in an assertion nor on any built-in meanings attached to specific symbol names. They are based strictly on symbol matching: constants must match themselves, and variables may be replaced with anything that allows a match to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may freely change token names (e.g., 'provable' instead of |-|) as long as you are consistent; correctness depends on consistent symbol usage and satisfying mandatory hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and token rules ($ keywords and comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only tokens built into the Metamath language are those beginning with $. These tokens are called 'keywords.' The Metamath token $( starts a comment and $) ends a comment. The $c, $v, $e, $f, $a, and $p tokens specify statements that end with $.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store source files as plain ASCII with line breaks; follow token spacing rules (tokens are separated by spaces or line breaks). When preparing files for different OSs, be careful about filename quoting and path syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display essential vs full construction views
rubrics_metrics.description: By default Metamath does not show $f hypotheses and everything branching off of them in the proof tree when the proof is displayed; this is called the 'essential' view. The /all qualifier displays the explicit construction of expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use essential view for human-readable logical steps, and /all or /lemmon /all when you need to inspect term/wff construction details for debugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed proof format for storage
rubrics_metrics.description: There is another proof format called 'compressed' that reduces the amount of space needed to store a proof in the database. A compressed proof can always be converted to a normal one and vice-versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize compressed proofs when encountering compact encodings in databases; use Metamath tools to convert or display them as readable normal proofs when needed.
